The '''variational multiscale method (VMS)''' is a technique used for deriving models and numerical methods for multiscale phenomena.<ref name="Hughes_Scovazzi_Franca_2004">{{cite book |last1=Hughes |first1=T.J.R. |last2=Scovazzi |first2=G. |last3=Franca |first3=L.P. |editor-last1=Stein |editor-first1=Erwin |editor-last2=de Borst |editor-first2=René |editor-last3=Hughes |editor-first3=Thomas J.R. |title=Encyclopedia of Computational Mechanics |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |date=2004 |pages=5–59 |chapter=Chapter 2: Multiscale and Stabilized Methods |isbn=0-470-84699-2}}</ref> The VMS framework has been mainly applied to design stabilized [[finite element method]]s in which stability of the standard [[Galerkin method]] is not ensured both in terms of [[singular perturbation]] and of compatibility conditions with the finite element spaces.<ref name="Codina_Badia_Baiges_Principe_2004">{{cite book |last1=Codina |first1=R. |last2=Badia |first2=S. |last3=Baiges |first3=J.  |last4=Principe |first4=J. |editor-last1=Stein |editor-first1=Erwin |editor-last2=de Borst |editor-first2=René |editor-last3=Hughes |editor-first3=Thomas J.R. |title=Encyclopedia of Computational Mechanics Second Edition|publisher=John Wiley & Sons |date=2017 |pages=1–28 |chapter=Chapter 2: Variational Multiscale Methods in Computational Fluid Dynamics| isbn=9781119003793}}</ref>

Stabilized methods are getting increasing attention in [[computational fluid dynamics]] because they are designed to solve drawbacks typical of the standard [[Galerkin method]]: advection-dominated flows problems and problems in which an arbitrary combination of interpolation functions may yield to unstable discretized formulations.<ref name="Masud_2004">{{cite journal |last1=Masud |first1=Arif |title=Preface |journal=Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering |date=April 2004 |volume=193 |issue=15–16 |pages=iii–iv |doi=10.1016/j.cma.2004.01.003}}</ref><ref name= "Quarteroni"/> The milestone of stabilized methods for this class of problems can be considered the Streamline Upwind Petrov-Galerkin method (SUPG), designed during 80s for convection dominated-flows for the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations by Brooks and Hughes.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Brooks |first1=Alexander N. |last2=Hughes |first2=Thomas J.R. |title=Streamline upwind/Petrov-Galerkin formulations for convection dominated flows with particular emphasis on the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations |journal=Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering |date=September 1982 |volume=32 |issue=1–3 |pages=199–259 |doi=10.1016/0045-7825(82)90071-8|bibcode=1982CMAME..32..199B }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Masud |first1=Arif |last2=Calderer |first2=Ramon |title=A variational multiscale stabilized formulation for the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations |journal=Computational Mechanics |date=3 February 2009 |volume=44 |issue=2 |pages=145–160 |doi=10.1007/s00466-008-0362-3|bibcode=2009CompM..44..145M |s2cid=7036642 }}</ref> Variational Multiscale Method (VMS) was introduced by Hughes in 1995.<ref name="Hughes_2005"/> Broadly speaking, VMS is a technique used to get mathematical models and numerical methods which are able to catch multiscale phenomena;<ref name= "Hughes_Scovazzi_Franca_2004" /> in fact, it is usually adopted for problems with huge scale ranges, which are separated into a number of scale groups.<ref name="Rasthofer_Gravemeier_2017">{{cite journal |last1=Rasthofer |first1=Ursula |last2=Gravemeier |first2=Volker |title=Recent Developments in Variational Multiscale Methods for Large-Eddy Simulation of Turbulent Flow |journal=Archives of Computational Methods in Engineering |date=27 February 2017 |volume=25 |issue=3 |pages=647–690 |doi=10.1007/s11831-017-9209-4|s2cid=29169067 |hdl=20.500.11850/129122 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> The main idea of the method is to design a sum decomposition of the solution as <math> u = \bar u + u' </math>, where <math> \bar u </math> is denoted as coarse-scale solution and it is solved numerically, whereas <math> u' </math> represents the fine scale solution and is determined analytically eliminating it from the problem of the coarse scale equation.<ref name= "Hughes_Scovazzi_Franca_2004" />

== The abstract framework ==

===Abstract Dirichlet problem with variational formulation===

Consider an open bounded domain <math>\Omega \subset \mathbb R^d </math> with smooth boundary <math>\Gamma \subset \mathbb R^{d-1} </math>, being <math> d \geq 1 </math> the number of space dimensions. Denoting with <math> \mathcal L </math> a generic, second order, nonsymmetric differential operator, consider the following [[boundary value problem]]:<ref name="Quarteroni" />  
:<math>
\text{find  } u: \Omega \to \mathbb R \text{ such that}:
</math>
:<math>
\begin{cases}
\mathcal L u = f & \text{ in } \Omega \\
u = g & \text{ on } \Gamma\\
\end{cases}
</math>

being <math>f: \Omega \to \mathbb R </math> and <math>g: \Gamma \to \mathbb R </math> given functions. Let  <math> H^1 (\Omega)</math> be the [[Hilbert space]] of square-integrable functions with square-integrable derivatives:<ref name="Quarteroni"/> 
:<math>
H^1(\Omega)= \{ f \in L^2(\Omega): \nabla f \in L^2 (\Omega)\}.
</math>
Consider the trial solution space <math> \mathcal V_g </math> and the weighting function space  <math> \mathcal V </math> defined as follows:<ref name="Quarteroni"/>

:<math>
\mathcal V_g = \{u \in H^1 (\Omega): \, u=g \text{ on } \Gamma \},
</math>

:<math>
\mathcal V =  H_0^1(\Omega) = \{v \in H^1 (\Omega): \, v=0 \text{ on } \Gamma \}.
</math>

The [[Weak formulation|variational formulation]] of the boundary value problem defined above reads:<ref name="Quarteroni"/>

:<math> \text{find }  u \in \mathcal V_g \text{ such that: } a(v, u) = f(v) \, \, \, \, \forall v \in \mathcal V </math>,

being <math> a(v, u) </math> the [[bilinear form]] satisfying <math> a(v, u) = (v, \mathcal L u) </math>, <math> f(v)=(v, f) </math> a bounded linear functional on <math> \mathcal V </math> and <math> (\cdot, \cdot) </math> is the <math> L^2(\Omega) </math> inner product.<ref name="Codina_Badia_Baiges_Principe_2004"/> Furthermore, the dual operator <math> \mathcal L^* </math> of <math> \mathcal L </math> is defined as that differential operator such that <math> \mathcal (v, \mathcal L u) = (\mathcal L^*v, u)\, \, \, \forall u, \, v \in \mathcal V </math>.<ref name="Hughes_2005"/>

===Variational multiscale method===
[[File:VMS figure.png|thumb|upright=2.0| One dimensional representation of <math>u</math>, <math>\bar u</math> and <math>u'</math>]]
In VMS approach, the function spaces are decomposed through a multiscale direct sum decomposition for both <math>\mathcal V_g</math> and <math>\mathcal V </math> into coarse and fine scales subspaces as:<ref name = "Hughes_Scovazzi_Franca_2004" />
:<math> 
\mathcal V= \bar {\mathcal V} \oplus \mathcal V' 
</math> 
and
:<math> 
\mathcal V_g= \bar {\mathcal V_g} \oplus \mathcal V_g'. 
</math>

Hence, an ''overlapping'' sum decomposition is assumed for both <math> u </math> and <math> v </math> as:

:<math> u = \bar{u} + u' \text{ and } v = \bar{v} + v'</math>,

where <math> \bar u </math> represents the ''coarse'' (resolvable) scales and <math> u' </math> the ''fine'' (subgrid) scales, with <math> \bar{u} \in \bar{\mathcal V_g} </math>, <math> {u'} \in {\mathcal V_g}' </math>,  <math> \bar{v} \in \bar{\mathcal V} </math> and <math> v' \in {\mathcal V}' </math>. In particular, the following assumptions are made on these functions:<ref name = "Hughes_Scovazzi_Franca_2004" />

:<math>
\begin{align}
\bar u = g & & \text{ on } \Gamma & & \forall& \bar u \in \bar{\mathcal{V_g}}, \\
u' = 0     & & \text{ on } \Gamma & & \forall& u' \in {\mathcal{V_g}}', \\
\bar v = 0 & & \text{ on } \Gamma & & \forall& \bar v \in \bar{\mathcal{V}}, \\
v' = 0     & & \text{ on } \Gamma & & \forall& v' \in {\mathcal{V}}'.
\end{align}
</math>

With this in mind, the variational form can be rewritten as

:<math>
a(\bar v + v', \bar u + u') = f (\bar v + v')
</math>

and, by using bilinearity of <math> a (\cdot , \cdot) </math> and linearity of <math> f (\cdot) </math>,

:<math>
a (\bar v, \bar u) + a (\bar v, u') + a (v', \bar u) + a(v', u') = f(\bar v) + f (v').
</math>

Last equation, yields to a coarse scale and a fine scale problem:

:<math>
\text{find } \bar u \in \bar{\mathcal V}_g \text{ and } u' \in \mathcal V' \text{ such that: }
</math>
:<math>
\begin{align}
& & a (\bar v, \bar u) + a (\bar v, u') &= f(\bar v) & & \forall \bar v \in \bar{\mathcal V} & \, \, \, \, \text{coarse-scale problem}\\
& & a (v', \bar u) + a (v', u') &= f( v') & & \forall  v' \in {\mathcal V}' & \, \, \, \, \text{fine-scale problem} \\
\end{align}
</math>
or, equivalently, considering that  <math> a(v, u) = (v, \mathcal L u) </math> and <math> f(v)=(v, f) </math>:
:<math>
\text{find } \bar u \in \bar{\mathcal V}_g \text{ and } u' \in \mathcal V' \text{ such that: }
</math>
:<math>
\begin{align}
& & (\bar v, \mathcal L \bar u) + (\bar v, \mathcal L u') &= (\bar v, f) & & \forall \bar v \in \bar{\mathcal V}, \\
& & (v', \mathcal L \bar u) + (v', \mathcal L u') &= ( v', f) & & \forall  v' \in {\mathcal V}'.\\
\end{align}
</math>
By rearranging the second problem as <math> (v', \mathcal L u') = - (v', \mathcal L \bar u - f) </math>, the corresponding [[Euler–Lagrange equation]] reads:<ref name="Hughes_2005"/>
:<math>
\begin{cases}
\mathcal L u' = - (\mathcal L \bar u - f) & \text{ in } \Omega \\
u' = 0 & \text{ on } \Gamma
\end{cases}
</math>
which shows that the fine scale solution <math> u' </math> depends on the strong residual of the coarse scale equation <math> \mathcal L \bar u - f </math>.<ref name="Hughes_2005">{{cite journal |last1=Hughes |first1=Thomas J.R. |title=Multiscale phenomena: Green's functions, the Dirichlet-to-Neumann formulation, subgrid scale models, bubbles and the origins of stabilized methods |journal=Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering |date=November 1995 |volume=127 |issue=1–4 |pages=387–401 |doi=10.1016/0045-7825(95)00844-9|bibcode=1995CMAME.127..387H |doi-access=free }}</ref> The fine scale solution can be expressed in terms of <math> \mathcal L \bar u - f </math> through the [[Green's function]] <math>G: \Omega \times \Omega \to \mathbb R \text{ with } G=0 \text{ on } \Gamma \times \Gamma </math>:
:<math>
u'(y) = - \int_\Omega G(x, y) (\mathcal L \bar u - f )(x)\,d \Omega_x \, \, \, \forall y \in \Omega.
</math>
Let <math> \delta</math> be the [[Dirac delta function]], by definition, the Green's function is found by solving <math> \forall y \in \Omega </math>
:<math> 
\begin{cases}
\mathcal L^* G(x, y) = \delta (x-y) & \text{ in } \Omega \\
G(x,y)=0 & \text{ on } \Gamma
\end{cases}
</math>
Moreover, it is possible to express <math> u' </math> in terms of a new differential operator <math> \mathcal M </math> that approximates the differential operator <math> - \mathcal L^{-1} </math> as <ref name = "Hughes_Scovazzi_Franca_2004" /> 
:
<math> 
u' = \mathcal M (\mathcal L \bar u - f),
</math>
with <math> \mathcal M \approx - \mathcal L^{-1}</math>. In order to eliminate the explicit dependence in the coarse scale equation of the sub-grid scale terms, considering the definition of the dual operator, the last expression can be substituted in the second term of the coarse scale equation:<ref name = "Hughes_Scovazzi_Franca_2004" /> 
:<math>
(\bar v, \mathcal L u') = (\mathcal L^* \bar v, u') = (\mathcal L^* \bar v,  \mathcal M (\mathcal L \bar u - f)).
</math>
Since <math> \mathcal M </math> is an approximation of <math> - \mathcal L^{-1} </math>, the Variational Multiscale Formulation will consist in finding an approximate solution <math> \tilde{\bar u} \approx \bar u </math> instead of <math> \bar u </math>. The coarse problem is therefore rewritten as:<ref name = "Hughes_Scovazzi_Franca_2004" /> 
:<math>
\text{find } \tilde{\bar u} \in \mathcal{\bar V}_g: \; \; \;  a (\bar v, \tilde{\bar u}) + (\mathcal L^* \bar v,  \mathcal M (\mathcal L \tilde{\bar u} - f)) = (\bar v, f) \; \; \; \forall \bar{v} \in \mathcal {\bar V},
</math>
being 
:<math>
(\mathcal L^* \bar v,  \mathcal M (\mathcal L \tilde{\bar u} - f)) = - \int_{\Omega} \int_{\Omega} (\mathcal L^* \bar v)(y) G(x, y) (\mathcal L \tilde{\bar u} - f)(x) \,d \Omega_x \,d\Omega_y.
</math>
Introducing the form <ref name="Hughes_2005"/> 
:<math> 
B(\bar v, \tilde{\bar u}, G) = a (\bar v, \tilde{\bar u}) + (\mathcal L^* \bar v,  \mathcal M (\mathcal L \tilde{\bar u})) 
</math> 
and the functional 
:<math> 
L(\bar v, G)= (\bar v, f) + (\mathcal L^* \bar v,  \mathcal M f) 
</math>, 
the VMS formulation of the coarse scale equation is rearranged as:<ref name="Hughes_2005"/> 
:<math>
\text{find } \tilde{\bar u} \in \mathcal{\bar V}_g: \, B(\bar v, \tilde{\bar u}, G) =  L(\bar v, G) \, \, \, \forall \bar{v} \in \mathcal {\bar V}.
</math>
Since commonly it is not possible to determine both <math> \mathcal M </math> and <math> G </math>, one usually adopt an approximation. In this sense, the coarse scale spaces <math>\bar{\mathcal V}_g</math> and <math>\bar{\mathcal V}</math> are chosen as finite dimensional space of functions as:<ref name = "Hughes_Scovazzi_Franca_2004" />
:<math>
\bar{\mathcal V}_g \equiv \mathcal V_{g_h} : = \mathcal V_g \cap X_r^h(\Omega) 
</math>
and
:<math>
 \bar{\mathcal V} \equiv \mathcal V_{h} : = \mathcal V \cap X_h^r(\Omega),
</math>
being <math>X_r^h(\Omega)</math> the Finite Element space of Lagrangian polynomials of degree <math> r \geq 1 </math> over the mesh built in <math> \Omega </math> .<ref name="Quarteroni">{{cite book |author-link1= Alfio Quarteroni |last1=Quarteroni |first1=Alfio |title=Numerical models for differential problems |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-319-49316-9 |edition=Third |date=2017-10-10 }}</ref> Note that <math> \mathcal{V}_g' </math> and <math> \mathcal{V}' </math> are infinite-dimensional spaces, while <math> \mathcal{V}_{g_h} </math> and <math> \mathcal{V}_h </math> are finite-dimensional spaces.

Let <math> u_h \in \mathcal V_{g_h} </math> and <math> v_h \in \mathcal V_{h} </math> be respectively approximations of <math> \tilde{\bar u} </math> and <math> {\bar v} </math>, and let <math> \tilde G </math> and <math> \tilde{\mathcal M}</math> be respectively approximations of <math>  G </math> and <math> {\mathcal M}</math>. The VMS problem with Finite Element approximation reads:<ref name="Hughes_2005"/> 
:<math>
\text{find } u_h \in \mathcal V_{g_h}: B(v_h, u_h, \tilde G) =  L( v_h, \tilde G) \, \, \, \forall {v}_h \in \mathcal { V}_h
</math> 
or, equivalently:
:<math>
\text{find } u_h \in \mathcal V_{g_h}: a (v_h, u_h) + (\mathcal L^*  v_h,  \mathcal {\tilde{M}} (\mathcal L { u_h} - f)) = ( v_h, f) \, \, \, \forall {v}_h \in \mathcal { V}_h
</math>

== VMS and stabilized methods ==

Consider an [[convection–diffusion equation|advection–diffusion]] problem:<ref name="Quarteroni" /> 
:<math>
\begin{cases}
-\mu \Delta u + \boldsymbol b \cdot \nabla u = f & \text{ in } \Omega \\
u=0 & \text{ on } \partial \Omega
\end{cases}
</math>
where <math> \mu \in \mathbb R </math> is the diffusion coefficient with <math> \mu>0 </math> and <math> \boldsymbol b \in \mathbb R^d </math> is a given advection field. Let <math> \mathcal{V}= H^1_0(\Omega) </math> and <math> u \in \mathcal V </math>, <math> \boldsymbol b \in [L^2(\Omega)]^d </math>, <math> f \in L^2(\Omega) </math>.<ref name="Quarteroni"/> Let <math> \mathcal L = \mathcal L_{diff} + \mathcal L_{adv} </math>, being <math> \mathcal L_{diff} = - \mu \Delta </math> and <math> \mathcal L_{adv} = \boldsymbol b \cdot \nabla </math>.<ref name="Hughes_Scovazzi_Franca_2004"/>
The variational form of the problem above reads:<ref name= "Quarteroni"/> 
:<math>
\text{find} \, u \in \mathcal V: \; \; \; a(v, u) = (f, v) \; \; \; \forall v \in \mathcal V,
</math>
being
:<math>
a(v, u) = (\nabla v, \mu \nabla u) + (v, \boldsymbol b \cdot \nabla u).
</math>
Consider a Finite Element approximation in space of the problem above by introducing the space <math> \mathcal V_h = \mathcal V \cap X_h^r </math> over a grid <math> \Omega_h = \bigcup_{k=1}^{N} \Omega_k </math> made of <math> N </math> elements, with <math> u_h \in \mathcal V_h </math>.

The standard Galerkin formulation of this problem reads<ref name= "Quarteroni"/>
:<math>
\text{find } u_h \in \mathcal V_h: \; \; \; a(v_h, u_h) = (f, v_h) \; \; \; \forall v \in \mathcal V,
</math>
Consider a strongly consistent stabilization method of the problem above in a finite element framework: 
:<math>
\text{ find } u_h \in \mathcal V_h: \, \, \, a(v_h, u_h) + \mathcal L_h (u_h, f; v_h)= (f, v_h) \, \, \, \forall v_h \in \mathcal V_h
</math>
for a suitable form <math> \mathcal L_h </math> that satisfies:<ref name="Quarteroni"/> 
:<math>
\mathcal L_h (u, f; v_h) = 0 \, \, \, \forall v_h \in \mathcal V_h.
</math>
The form <math> \mathcal L_h </math> can be expressed as <math> (\mathbb L v_h, \tau (\mathcal L u_h - f))_{\Omega_h} </math>, being <math> \mathbb L </math> a differential operator such as:<ref name="Hughes_Scovazzi_Franca_2004"/>
:<math>
\mathbb L=
\begin{cases}
+ \mathcal L & \, \, \, & \text{ Galerkin/least squares (GLS)} \\
+ \mathcal L_{adv} & \, \, \, & \text{ Streamline Upwind Petrov-Galerkin (SUPG)} \\
- \mathcal L^* & \, \, \, & \text{ Multiscale} \\
\end{cases}
</math>
and <math> \tau </math> is the stabilization parameter. A stabilized method with <math> \mathbb L = -\mathcal L^* </math> is typically referred to '''multiscale stabilized method '''. In 1995, [[Thomas J.R. Hughes]] showed that a stabilized method of multiscale type can be viewed as a sub-grid scale model where the stabilization parameter is equal to 
:<math> 
\tau= - \tilde{\mathcal M} \approx - \mathcal M 
</math>
or, in terms of the Green's function as
:<math>
\tau \delta (x-y) = \tilde G(x, y) \approx G(x,y),
</math>
which yields the following definition of <math> \tau </math>: 
:<math>
\tau = \frac{1}{|\Omega_k|} \int_{\Omega_k} \int_{\Omega_k} G(x, y) \,d\Omega_x \,d\Omega_y.
</math><ref name="Hughes_2005"/>

=== Stabilization Parameter Properties ===
For the 1-d advection diffusion problem, with an appropriate choice of basis functions and <math>\tau</math>, VMS provides a projection in the approximation space.<ref>{{cite journal |last1= Hughes|first1= T.J.|last2= Sangalli|first2= G.|title= Variational multiscale analysis: the fine-scale Green's function, projection, optimization, localization, and stabilized methods|journal= SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis|date= 2007|volume= 45|issue= 2|pages= 539–557|publisher= SIAM |doi= 10.1137/050645646}}</ref> Further, an adjoint-based expression for <math>\tau</math> can be derived,<ref name="Garg_Stogner_CMAME_2019">{{cite journal |last1= Garg|first1= V.V.|last2= Stogner |first2= R.|title= Local enhancement of functional evaluation and adjoint error estimation for variational multiscale formulations|journal= Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering|date= 2019|volume= 354|pages= 119–142| publisher= Elsevier|doi= 10.1016/j.cma.2019.05.023}}</ref>
:<math>
\tau_e = -\frac{\mathcal L(\tilde{z}, u_h)_e}{(\phi_{e}L_h(u_h)),L^*(\tilde{z}))_e}
</math>
where <math>\tau_e</math> is the element wise stabilization parameter, <math>\mathcal L(\tilde{z}, u_h)_e</math> is the element wise residual and the adjoint <math>\tilde{z}</math> problem solves,
:<math>
\mathcal a(\tilde{z}, v) + L_h(\tilde{z}, v) = \int_{\Omega_e} v \, dx
</math>
In fact, one can show that the <math>\tau</math> thus calculated allows one to compute the linear functional <math> \int_{\Omega} u \, dx </math> exactly.<ref name="Garg_Stogner_CMAME_2019" />

== VMS turbulence modeling for large-eddy simulations of incompressible flows ==

The idea of VMS [[turbulence modeling]] for Large Eddy Simulations([[Large eddy simulation|LES]]) of incompressible [[Navier–Stokes equations]] was introduced by Hughes et al. in 2000 and the main idea was to use - instead of classical filtered techniques - variational projections.<ref name="Hughes_Mazzei_Jansen_2000">{{cite journal |last1=Hughes |first1=Thomas J.R. |last2=Mazzei |first2=Luca |last3=Jansen |first3=Kenneth E. |title=Large Eddy Simulation and the variational multiscale method |journal=Computing and Visualization in Science |date=May 2000 |volume=3 |issue=1–2 |pages=47–59 |doi=10.1007/s007910050051|s2cid=120207183 }}</ref><ref name="Bazilevs_Calo_Cottrell_Hughes_Scovazzi_2007">{{cite journal |last1=Bazilevs |first1=Y. |last2=Calo |first2=V.M. |last3=Cottrell |first3=J.A. |last4=Hughes |first4=T.J.R. |last5=Reali |first5=A. |last6=Scovazzi |first6=G. |title=Variational multiscale residual-based turbulence modeling for large eddy simulation of incompressible flows |journal=Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering |date=December 2007 |volume=197 |issue=1–4 |pages=173–201 |doi=10.1016/j.cma.2007.07.016|bibcode=2007CMAME.197..173B }}</ref>

=== Incompressible Navier–Stokes equations ===
Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations for a [[Newtonian fluid]] of constant [[density]] <math> \rho </math> in a domain <math> \Omega \in \mathbb R^d </math> with boundary <math> \partial \Omega = \Gamma_D \cup \Gamma_N </math>, being <math> \Gamma_D </math> and <math> \Gamma_N </math> portions of the boundary where respectively a [[Dirichlet boundary condition|Dirichlet]] and a [[Neumann boundary condition]]  is applied (<math> \Gamma_D \cap \Gamma_N = \emptyset </math>):<ref name = "Quarteroni" />
:<math>
\begin{cases}
\rho \dfrac{\partial \boldsymbol u}{\partial t} + \rho (\boldsymbol u \cdot \nabla) \boldsymbol u - \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol \sigma (\boldsymbol u, p) = \boldsymbol f & \text{ in } \Omega \times (0, T) \\
\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol u = 0  & \text{ in } \Omega \times (0, T) \\
\boldsymbol u = \boldsymbol g & \text{ on } \Gamma_D \times (0, T) \\
 \sigma (\boldsymbol u, p) \boldsymbol{\hat n} = \boldsymbol h & \text{ on } \Gamma_N \times (0, T) \\
\boldsymbol u(0)= \boldsymbol u_0 & \text{ in } \Omega \times \{ 0\}
\end{cases}
</math>
being <math> \boldsymbol u </math> the fluid velocity, <math> p </math> the fluid pressure, <math> \boldsymbol f </math> a given forcing term, <math> \boldsymbol{\hat n} </math> the outward directed unit normal vector to <math> \Gamma_N </math>, and <math> \boldsymbol \sigma (\boldsymbol u, p) </math> the [[viscous stress tensor]] defined as: 
:<math>
\boldsymbol \sigma (\boldsymbol u, p) = -p \boldsymbol I + 2 \mu \boldsymbol \epsilon (\boldsymbol u).
</math>
Let <math> \mu </math> be the dynamic viscosity of the fluid, <math> \boldsymbol I </math> the second order [[Identity matrix|identity tensor]] and <math> \boldsymbol \epsilon (\boldsymbol u) </math> the [[strain-rate tensor]] defined as: 
:<math>
\boldsymbol \epsilon (\boldsymbol u) = \frac{1}{2} ((\nabla \boldsymbol u) + (\nabla \boldsymbol u)^T).
</math>
The functions <math> \boldsymbol g </math> and <math> \boldsymbol h </math> are given Dirichlet and Neumann boundary data, while <math> \boldsymbol u_0 </math> is the [[initial condition]].<ref name= "Quarteroni"/>

=== Global space time variational formulation ===

In order to find a variational formulation of the Navier–Stokes equations, consider the following infinite-dimensional spaces:<ref name="Quarteroni"/> 
:<math> 
\mathcal  V_g= \{ \boldsymbol u \in [H^1(\Omega)]^d : \boldsymbol u = \boldsymbol g \text{ on } \Gamma_D \}, 
</math>
:<math> 
\mathcal  V_0 = [H^1_0(\Omega)]^d=\{ \boldsymbol u \in [H^1(\Omega)]^d : \boldsymbol u = \boldsymbol 0 \text{ on } \Gamma_D \}, 
</math>
:<math> 
\mathcal Q =L^2(\Omega).
</math>
Furthermore, let <math> \boldsymbol \mathcal V_g = \mathcal  V_g \times \mathcal Q </math> and <math> \boldsymbol \mathcal V_0 = \mathcal  V_0 \times \mathcal Q </math>. The weak form of the unsteady-incompressible Navier–Stokes equations reads:<ref name="Quarteroni"/> given <math> \boldsymbol u_{0}</math>,
:<math>
\forall t \in (0, T), \; \text{find } (\boldsymbol u, p) \in \boldsymbol \mathcal V_g \text{ such that } 
</math>
:<math>
\begin{align}
\bigg( \boldsymbol v, \rho \dfrac{\partial \boldsymbol u}{\partial t}\bigg) + a (\boldsymbol v, \boldsymbol u) + c (\boldsymbol v, \boldsymbol u, \boldsymbol u) - b (\boldsymbol v, p) + b (\boldsymbol u, q) = (\boldsymbol v, \boldsymbol f) + (\boldsymbol v, \boldsymbol h)_{\Gamma_N} \; \; \forall (\boldsymbol v, q) \in \boldsymbol \mathcal V_0
\end{align}
</math>
where <math> (\cdot, \cdot) </math> represents the <math> L^2(\Omega) </math> inner product and <math> (\cdot, \cdot)_{\Gamma_N} </math> the <math> L^2(\Gamma_N) </math> inner product. Moreover, the bilinear forms <math> a(\cdot, \cdot) </math>, <math> b(\cdot, \cdot) </math> and the trilinear form <math> c(\cdot, \cdot, \cdot) </math> are defined as follows:<ref name="Quarteroni"/>
:<math>
\begin{align}
a (\boldsymbol v, \boldsymbol u) = & (\nabla \boldsymbol v, \mu ((\nabla \boldsymbol u) + (\nabla \boldsymbol u)^T)), \\
b (\boldsymbol v, q) = &(\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol v, q), \\
c (\boldsymbol v, \boldsymbol u, \boldsymbol u) = &(\boldsymbol v, \rho (\boldsymbol u \cdot \nabla) \boldsymbol u). 
\end{align}
</math>

===Finite element method for space discretization and VMS-LES modeling===
In order to discretize in space the Navier–Stokes equations, consider the function space of finite element
:<math>
X_r^h = \{u^h \in C^0 (\overline\Omega): u^h|_k \in \mathbb P_r, \; \forall k \in \Tau_h\}
</math>
of piecewise Lagrangian Polynomials of degree <math> r \geq 1 </math> over the domain <math> \Omega </math> triangulated with a mesh <math> \Tau_h</math> made of tetrahedrons of diameters <math> h_k </math>, <math> \forall k \in \Tau_h </math>. 
Following the approach shown above, let introduce a multiscale direct-sum decomposition of the space <math>\boldsymbol \mathcal V </math> which represents either <math>\boldsymbol \mathcal V_g</math> and <math>\boldsymbol \mathcal V_0</math>:<ref name="Forti_Dede_2015" >{{cite journal |last1=Forti |first1=Davide |last2=Dedè |first2=Luca |title=Semi-implicit BDF time discretization of the Navier–Stokes equations with VMS-LES modeling in a High Performance Computing framework |journal=Computers & Fluids |date=August 2015 |volume=117 |pages=168–182 |doi=10.1016/j.compfluid.2015.05.011}}</ref>
:<math>
\boldsymbol \mathcal V = \boldsymbol \mathcal V_h \oplus \boldsymbol \mathcal V',
</math>
being 
:<math> 
\boldsymbol \mathcal V_h = \mathcal V_{g_h} \times \mathcal Q \text{ or } \boldsymbol  \mathcal V_h = \mathcal V_{0_h} \times \mathcal Q 
</math>
the finite dimensional function space associated to the '''coarse scale''', and 
:<math> 
\boldsymbol \mathcal V' = \mathcal V_g' \times \mathcal Q  \text{ or } \boldsymbol \mathcal V' = \mathcal V_0' \times \mathcal Q 
</math>
the infinite-dimensional '''fine scale''' function space, with 
:<math> \mathcal V_{g_h}  = \mathcal V_g \cap X_r^h </math>, 
:<math> \mathcal V_{0_h}  = \mathcal V_0 \cap X_r^h </math> 
and 
:<math> \mathcal Q_h  = \mathcal Q \cap X_r^h </math>. 
An overlapping sum decomposition is then defined as:<ref name="Bazilevs_Calo_Cottrell_Hughes_Scovazzi_2007"/><ref name="Forti_Dede_2015"/>
:<math>
\begin{align}
& \boldsymbol u = \boldsymbol u^h + \boldsymbol u'  \text{ and } p = p^h + p' \\
& \boldsymbol v = \boldsymbol v^h + \boldsymbol v'  \;\text{ and } q = q^h + q' 
\end{align}
</math>
By using the decomposition above in the variational form of the Navier–Stokes equations, one gets a coarse and a fine scale equation; the fine scale terms appearing in the coarse scale equation are [[Integration by parts|integrated by parts]] and the fine scale variables are modeled as:<ref name="Bazilevs_Calo_Cottrell_Hughes_Scovazzi_2007"/>
:<math>
\begin{align}
\boldsymbol u' \approx & -\tau_M (\boldsymbol u^h) \boldsymbol r_M (\boldsymbol u^h, p^h), \\
p' \approx & -\tau_C (\boldsymbol u^h) \boldsymbol r_C (\boldsymbol u^h).
\end{align}
</math>
In the expressions above, <math>\boldsymbol r_M (\boldsymbol u^h, p^h) </math> and <math> \boldsymbol r_C (\boldsymbol u^h) </math> are the residuals of the momentum equation and continuity equation in strong forms defined as: 
:<math>
\begin{align}
\boldsymbol r_M (\boldsymbol u^h, p^h) = & \rho \dfrac{\partial \boldsymbol u^h}{\partial t} + \rho (\boldsymbol u^h \cdot \nabla) \boldsymbol u^h - \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol \sigma (\boldsymbol u^h, p^h) - \boldsymbol f,\\
\boldsymbol r_C (\boldsymbol u^h) = & \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol u^h,
\end{align}
</math>
while the stabilization parameters are set equal to:<ref name="Forti_Dede_2015"/>
:<math>
\begin{align}
\tau_M (\boldsymbol u^h) = & \bigg ( \frac{\sigma^2 \rho^2}{\Delta t^2} + \frac{\rho^2 }{h_k^2} |\boldsymbol u^h|^2 + \frac{\mu^2}{h_k^4}C_r\bigg )^{-1/2}, \\
\tau_C (\boldsymbol u^h) = & \frac{h_k^2}{\tau_M (\boldsymbol u^h) },
\end{align}
</math>
where <math> C_r = 60 \cdot 2^{r-2}</math> is a constant depending on the polynomials's degree <math> r </math>, <math> \sigma </math> is a constant equal to the order of the [[backward differentiation formula]] (BDF) adopted as temporal integration scheme and <math> \Delta t </math> is the time step.<ref name="Forti_Dede_2015"/> The semi-discrete variational multiscale multiscale formulation (VMS-LES) of the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations, reads:<ref name="Forti_Dede_2015"/> given <math> \boldsymbol u_{0}</math>,
:<math>
\forall t \in (0, T), \; \text{find } \boldsymbol U^h = \{\boldsymbol u^h, p^h\} \in \boldsymbol \mathcal V_{g_h} \text{ such that } A(\boldsymbol V^h, \boldsymbol U^h ) = F(\boldsymbol V^h) \; \; \forall \boldsymbol V^h= \{\boldsymbol v^h, q^h\} \in \boldsymbol \mathcal V_{0_h},
</math>
being 
:<math>
A(\boldsymbol V^h, \boldsymbol U^h ) = A^{NS}(\boldsymbol V^h, \boldsymbol U^h ) + A^{VMS}(\boldsymbol V^h, \boldsymbol U^h ),
</math>
and
:<math>
F(\boldsymbol V^h) = (\boldsymbol v, \boldsymbol f) + (\boldsymbol v, \boldsymbol h)_{\Gamma_N}.
</math>
The forms <math> A^{NS}(\cdot, \cdot) </math> and <math> A^{VMS}(\cdot, \cdot) </math> are defined as:<ref name="Forti_Dede_2015"/> 
:<math>
\begin{align}
A^{NS}(\boldsymbol V^h, \boldsymbol U^h )= & \bigg( \boldsymbol v^h, \rho \dfrac{\partial \boldsymbol u^h}{\partial t}\bigg) + a (\boldsymbol v^h, \boldsymbol u^h) + c (\boldsymbol v^h, \boldsymbol u^h, \boldsymbol u^h) - b (\boldsymbol v^h, p^h) + b (\boldsymbol u^h, q^h), \\
A^{VMS}(\boldsymbol V^h, \boldsymbol U^h ) = & \underbrace{\big( \rho \boldsymbol u^h \cdot \nabla \boldsymbol v^h + \nabla q^h, \tau_M(\boldsymbol u^h) \boldsymbol r_M(\boldsymbol u^h, p^h) \big)}_{\text{SUPG}}   -    \underbrace{(\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol v^h, \tau_c(\boldsymbol u_h)\boldsymbol r_C(\boldsymbol u^h))   +    \big( \rho \boldsymbol u^h \cdot (\nabla \boldsymbol u^h)^T, \tau_M(\boldsymbol u^h) \boldsymbol r_M (\boldsymbol u^h, p^h)  \big )}_{\text{VMS}}   -    \underbrace{(\nabla \boldsymbol v^h, \tau_M(\boldsymbol u^h) \boldsymbol r_M(\boldsymbol u^h, p^h) \otimes \tau_M(\boldsymbol u^h) \boldsymbol r_M(\boldsymbol u^h, p^h) )}_{\text{LES}}.
\end{align}
</math>
From the expressions above, one can see that:<ref name="Forti_Dede_2015"/> 
* the form <math>A^{NS}(\cdot, \cdot)</math> contains the standard terms of the Navier–Stokes equations in variational formulation; 
* the form <math>A^{VMS}(\cdot, \cdot)</math> contain four terms: 
# the first term is the classical SUPG stabilization term; 
# the second term represents a stabilization term additional to the SUPG one; 
# the third term is a stabilization term typical of the VMS modeling; 
# the fourth term is peculiar of the LES modeling, describing the Reynolds cross-stress.
